builder_plan.scenario: An agent reads external documents or tool responses that may contain malicious instructions.
builder_plan.change: Replay attacks and legitimate lookalikes in an isolated copy of your agent workflow.
builder_plan.baseline: Your existing checks with the same tasks, permissions, and tool responses.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Successful attacks missed, legitimate actions blocked, detection delay, and review cost.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
summary: The technique replaces indiscriminate agent attacks with a multi-agent co-design that pairs MCP status tools (which return accurate status and terminate normally) with completion-confirmation prompts to exploit the agent's autonomous completion decisions. It costs the attacker the complexity of maintaining a multi-agent framework and separate tool and prompt reviews; for the victim SaaS provider, it increases API request consumption and resource usage without additional customer payment. For a defender, implementing countermeasures (budget caps, loop detection, verification of completion) adds operational overhead. What can fail after adoption of defenses: OverServe's tool specifications trigger no alerts in evaluated MCP scanners, so existing scanning tools may miss these attacks, and agents may still repeatedly check unfinished conditions despite task completion.
rationale: This paper demonstrates a concrete, high-magnitude denial-of-wallet threat to subscription SaaS agents; providers should test resource limits and completion verification since MCP scanners currently fail to detect such attacks.
technique: Tool–prompt co-design resource amplification attacks on SaaS agents
